title: Application of the Border Gateway Protocol in the Internet
summary: Describes how the Border Gateway Protocol is used in the Internet, as the companion to RFC 1771. It covers how BGP fits into inter-autonomous-system routing. It was a draft standard.

plainLanguage.summary: BGP is the protocol routers use to tell each other which networks they can reach. This document explains how it is meant to be used: how the networks are grouped into autonomous systems, how routes are aggregated and filtered by policy, and how the best of several possible paths is chosen.

questions: how is bgp used in the internet
what does rfc 1772 say about route aggregation
subtitle: How BGP-4 is meant to be used between autonomous systems: topology, route aggregation, policy and path selection.

tldr.problem: The Internet was running out of address space and the routing tables were growing faster than the software and the people who ran them could manage.
tldr.mechanism: BGP exchanges reachability information together with the full path of autonomous systems the traffic crosses, so loops can be detected, and it applies policy from configuration rather than from the protocol itself. Route aggregation lets a router advertise one prefix for a block of addresses it administers.
tldr.outcome: The document is the usage half of BGP-4, sitting beside the protocol specification in RFC 1771. It describes the topological model, the policies that implementations should support, and how to migrate from EGP2 and BGP-3.

today: RFC 1772 is a Draft Standard from March 1995 that obsoletes RFC 1655, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The document describes how BGP-4 is used in the Internet; the protocol itself is specified in RFC 1771.

sections.title: The Scaling Problem and BGP-4
sections.content:
The document describes the use of BGP in the Internet environment. BGP is an inter-autonomous system routing protocol, and the network reachability information it exchanges provides enough information to detect routing loops and to enforce routing decisions based on performance preference and policy constraints. In particular, BGP exchanges routing information containing full AS paths and enforces routing policies based on configuration information.

As the Internet grew, it became clear that it faced several serious scaling problems. The class B network address space was close to exhausted, because class C, with a maximum of 254 host addresses, was too small for a mid-sized organisation while class B, which allows up to 65534 addresses, was too large to be densely populated. The growth of routing tables in Internet routers was beyond the ability of current software, and of the people running it, to manage effectively. Eventually the 32-bit IP address space would be exhausted too.

The first two problems were likely to become critical within one to three years. Classless inter-domain routing deals with them by proposing a mechanism to slow the growth of the routing table and the need for allocating new IP network numbers. It does not attempt to solve the third problem, which is of a more long-term nature, but rather eases enough of the short to mid-term difficulties to allow the Internet to continue to function efficiently while progress is made on a longer-term solution.

BGP-4 is an extension of BGP-3 that adds support for routing information aggregation and reduction based on the CIDR architecture. This document describes the usage of BGP-4 in the Internet.

All of the discussion rests on the assumption that the Internet is a collection of arbitrarily connected autonomous systems, modelled as a general graph whose nodes are autonomous systems and whose edges are connections between pairs of them. The classic definition of an autonomous system is a set of routers under a single technical administration, using an interior gateway protocol and common metrics to route packets within it and an exterior gateway protocol to route packets to other systems. Since that definition was developed it has become common for a single AS to use several interior gateway protocols, and sometimes several sets of metrics. The term stresses that, even when several IGPs and metrics are used, the administration of an AS appears to other AS's to have a single coherent interior routing plan and presents a consistent picture of which destinations are reachable through it.
sections.plainLanguage: BGP was written to slow the growth of the routing tables and to hold back the use of address space. It does that by letting one router advertise a single prefix for a block of addresses, and by attaching the whole path of networks to every route it advertises so that loops can be spotted.

sections.title: The Topological Model
sections.content:
A connection between two autonomous systems means two things. There is a physical connection, a shared data link subnetwork between the two AS's, on which each AS has at least one border gateway belonging to it, so that the border gateway of each AS can forward packets to the border gateway of the other AS without resorting to inter-AS or intra-AS routing. There is also a BGP connection, a BGP session between BGP speakers in each of the AS's, which communicates the routes that can be used for specific destinations via the advertising AS.

The document places an additional restriction on the BGP speakers that form a BGP connection: they must themselves share the same data link subnetwork that their border gateways share, so a BGP session between adjacent AS's needs no support from either inter-AS or intra-AS routing. Cases that do not conform fall outside the scope of the document. At each connection, each AS therefore has one or more BGP speakers and one or more border gateways, all on a shared data link subnetwork. BGP speakers do not need to be border gateways, and vice versa. Paths announced by a BGP speaker of one AS on a given connection are taken to be feasible for each of the border gateways of the other AS on the same shared subnetwork, so indirect neighbours are allowed.

Traffic carried within an AS either originates or terminates there, when the source or destination IP address of the packet identifies a host internal to that AS. Traffic that fits this description is called local traffic; traffic that does not is called transit traffic. A major goal of BGP usage is to control the flow of transit traffic, and the way an AS deals with transit traffic places it in one of three categories. A stub AS has only a single connection to one other AS, and so only carries local traffic. A multihomed AS has connections to more than one other AS but refuses to carry transit traffic. A transit AS has connections to more than one other AS and is designed, under certain policy restrictions, to carry both transit and local traffic.

Because a full AS path provides an efficient and straightforward way of suppressing routing loops and eliminates the count-to-infinity problem associated with some distance vector algorithms, BGP imposes no topological restrictions on the interconnection of AS's.
sections.plainLanguage: An autonomous system is one administration's network. The document sorts them three ways: a stub with a single link, a multihomed system with several links that will not carry other people's traffic, and a transit system that will. Traffic that starts and ends inside the system is local traffic; everything else is transit traffic.

sections.title: BGP in the Internet
sections.content:
The overall Internet topology may be viewed as an arbitrary interconnection of transit, multihomed and stub AS's. In order to minimise the impact on the current Internet infrastructure, stub and multihomed AS's need not use BGP; they may run other protocols such as EGP to exchange reachability information with transit AS's, and transit AS's using BGP will tag that information as having been learned by some method other than BGP. The fact that BGP need not run on stub or multihomed AS's has no negative impact on the overall quality of inter-AS routing for traffic destined to or originating from them. It is nevertheless recommended that BGP be used for stub and multihomed AS's as well, because it gives an advantage in bandwidth and performance over some of the protocols then in use, reduces the need for default routes, and gives better choices of inter-AS routes for multihomed AS's.

At a global level, BGP is used to distribute routing information among multiple autonomous systems. While BGP alone carries information between AS's, both BGP and an IGP may carry information across an AS, and ensuring consistency of routing information between BGP and an IGP within an AS is a significant issue, which Appendix A of the document discusses at length. The general rule it gives is that a border gateway should not advertise to any external peer a route to exterior destinations via another border gateway of the same AS until all the interior gateways within the AS are ready to route that traffic to the correct exit gateway. Otherwise, during the window before interior routing converges, either incorrect routing or black holes can occur.

Routers that communicate directly with each other via BGP are known as BGP speakers, and they can be located within the same AS or in different AS's. For a given BGP speaker, another speaker it communicates with is an external peer if that speaker is in a different AS, and an internal peer if it is in the same AS. There can be as many BGP speakers as are deemed necessary within an AS, and if an AS has multiple connections to other AS's, multiple BGP speakers are needed. All BGP speakers representing the same AS must give a consistent image of the AS to the outside, which requires them to have consistent routing information among them; they can communicate with each other via BGP or by other means. The policy constraints applied to all BGP speakers within an AS must be consistent, and techniques such as using a tagged IGP may be employed to detect possible inconsistencies. External peers must belong to different AS's but share a common data link subnetwork, which should be used to carry the BGP messages between them. The use of BGP across an intervening AS invalidates the AS path information, and an Autonomous System number must be used with BGP to specify which AS the BGP speaker belongs to.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet is an arbitrary mesh of autonomous systems. BGP can run between any two that share a link, and every router in one system has to present the same picture to the outside. The hard part is the handover inside a system: a router must not advertise a path outwards until the internal routing has caught up with it.

sections.title: Route Aggregation and Overlapping Routes
sections.content:
A conformant BGP-4 implementation must be able to specify when an aggregated route may be generated out of partial routing information. For example, a BGP speaker at the border of an autonomous system, or group of them, must be able to generate an aggregated route for a whole set of destination IP addresses, called in BGP-4 terminology the Network Layer Reachability Information or NLRI, over which it has administrative control, including those addresses it has delegated, even when not all of them are reachable at the same time. A conformant implementation may provide the capability to specify when an aggregated NLRI may be generated, and is required to have the ability to specify how NLRI may be de-aggregated.

A conformant implementation is required to support four options when dealing with overlapping routes: install both the less and the more specific routes, install the more specific route only, install the less specific route only, or install neither route.

Certain routing policies may depend on the NLRI, for example a research network distinguished from a commercial one, so a BGP speaker that performs route aggregation should be aware, if possible, of the implications for routing policies when it aggregates.
sections.plainLanguage: A router that owns a block of addresses can advertise the whole block as one route, even when some of it is not currently reachable. It has to be able to say when it does that, how to split the block back up, and what to do when two routes overlap.

sections.title: Policy Making with BGP
sections.content:
BGP provides the capability for enforcing policies based on various routing preferences and constraints. Policies are not directly encoded in the protocol; they are provided to BGP in the form of configuration information. BGP enforces policies by affecting the selection of paths from multiple alternatives and by controlling the redistribution of routing information. Policies are determined by the AS administration, and are related to political, security or economic considerations. For example, if an AS is unwilling to carry traffic to another AS, it can enforce a policy prohibiting this.

The examples of policies that can be enforced with BGP are: a multihomed AS can refuse to act as a transit AS for other AS's, by only advertising routes to destinations internal to the AS; a multihomed AS can become a transit AS for a restricted set of adjacent AS's, by advertising its routing information to that set of AS's only; and an AS can favour or disfavour the use of certain AS's for carrying transit traffic from itself.

A number of performance-related criteria can also be controlled. An AS can minimise the number of transit AS's by preferring shorter AS paths over longer ones. The quality of transit AS's can be taken into account: if an AS determines that two or more AS paths can be used to reach a given destination, it can use a variety of means to decide which candidate path it will use, and the quality of an AS can be measured by things such as diameter, link speed, capacity, tendency to become congested and quality of operation. Information about these qualities might be determined by means other than BGP. An AS can also express a preference of internal routes over external routes. For consistency within an AS, equal cost paths, resulting from combinations of policies and normal route selection procedures, must be resolved in a consistent fashion.

Fundamental to BGP is the rule that an AS advertises to its neighbouring AS's only those routes that it uses. This rule reflects the hop-by-hop routing paradigm generally used by the current Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: Policy lives in the configuration, not in the protocol. An operator uses it to decide what to advertise and which path to prefer, and the document gives examples: refusing to carry other people's traffic, preferring shorter paths, preferring faster neighbours, and preferring internal routes.

sections.title: Path Selection
sections.content:
One of the major tasks of a BGP speaker is to evaluate different paths from itself to a set of destinations covered by an address prefix, select the best one, apply appropriate policy constraints, and then advertise it to all of its BGP neighbours. The key issue is how different paths are evaluated and compared. In traditional distance vector protocols such as RIP there is only one metric, such as hop count, associated with a path, so comparison reduces to comparing two numbers. A complication in inter-AS routing arises from the lack of a universally agreed metric among AS's that can be used to evaluate external paths; each AS may have its own set of criteria.

A BGP speaker builds a routing database consisting of the set of all feasible paths and the list of destinations, expressed as address prefixes, reachable through each path. In most cases there is only one feasible path. When that is not the case, all feasible paths should be maintained, and maintaining them speeds adaptation to the loss of the primary path; only the primary path at any given time is ever advertised.

The process can be formalised by defining a complete order over the set of all feasible paths to a set of destinations associated with a given address prefix, for example by defining a function that maps each full AS path to a non-negative integer denoting the path's degree of preference. Path selection is then reduced to applying that function to all feasible paths and choosing the one with the highest degree of preference. In actual implementations the criteria are specified as configuration information.

The possible criteria for assigning a degree of preference to a path are: AS count, where paths with a smaller AS count are generally better; policy considerations, where a BGP speaker may know policy constraints within and outside its own AS and does appropriate path selection, and paths that do not comply with policy requirements are not considered further; the presence or absence of a certain AS in the path, using information from outside the scope of BGP, such as bandwidth, MTU or intra-AS diameter of certain AS's; path origin, where a path learned entirely from BGP is generally better than one for which part of the path was learned via EGP or another means; AS path subsets, where an AS path that is a subset of a longer AS path to the same destination should be preferred, because any problem in the shorter path is also a problem in the longer one; and link dynamics, where stable paths should be preferred over unstable ones, though this criterion must be used very carefully, since any criterion that depends on dynamic information might cause routing instability.
sections.plainLanguage: The router keeps every usable path it knows about, scores each one with a number of its own choosing, and advertises only the highest scorer. The document lists what can go into that score: how many networks the path crosses, whether policy allows it, whether a particular network is in the path, where the path came from, whether the path is a prefix of a longer one, and how stable it is.

sections.title: Required Routing Policies
sections.content:
Policies are provided to BGP in the form of configuration information, which is not directly encoded in the protocol, so BGP can support very complex routing policies. It is not required that all implementations support such policies, and the document does not attempt to standardise the policies that must be supported in every implementation. It does strongly encourage all implementors to support the following set.

  1. BGP implementations should allow an AS to control announcements of BGP-learned routes to adjacent AS's, with at least the granularity of a single address prefix, and also with the granularity of an autonomous system, which may be the AS that originated the route or the adjacent AS that advertised it. Care must be taken when a BGP speaker selects a new route that cannot be announced to a particular external peer while the previously selected route was announced to that peer: the local system must explicitly indicate to the peer that the previous route is now infeasible.
  2. BGP implementations should allow an AS to prefer a particular path to a destination when more than one is available. At the minimum an implementation shall support this by allowing a degree of preference to be assigned administratively to a route based solely on the IP address of the neighbour the route is received from, with the allowed range of that degree of preference between 0 and 2^31 - 1.
  3. BGP implementations should allow an AS to ignore routes with certain AS's in the AS_PATH path attribute. This can be done using the technique in RFC 1104, assigning infinity as the weight for such AS's, and the route selection process must ignore routes that have a weight equal to infinity.

The document's security considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in the memo, although Section 5 notes that routing policies are related to political, security or economic considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: The document does not insist on particular policies, but it asks every implementation to support three: being able to filter what is advertised and to whom, being able to prefer one path over another, and being able to refuse routes that pass through a named network.

sections.title: Interaction with Older Protocols and Switched Circuits
sections.content:
An AS should advertise a minimal aggregate for its internal destinations, with respect to the amount of address space it is actually using, and this can be used by administrators of non-BGP-4 AS's to determine how many routes to explode from a single aggregate. A route carrying the ATOMIC_AGGREGATE path attribute shall not be exported into either BGP-3 or EGP2 unless that can be done without exploding the NLRI of the route.

For a graceful migration, a BGP speaker may participate in EGP2 as well as in BGP-4, so it may receive reachability information by means of EGP2 as well as by means of BGP-4. Information received by EGP2 can be injected into BGP-4 with the ORIGIN path attribute set to 1, and information received via BGP-4 can be injected into EGP2. In the latter case one needs to be aware of the potential information explosion when a given IP prefix received from BGP-4 denotes a set of consecutive A, B or C class networks; injecting BGP-4 received NLRI that denotes IP subnets requires the speaker to inject the corresponding network into EGP2. A conformant implementation must support three options when injecting BGP-4 received reachability information into EGP2: inject the default only, 0.0.0.0, with no export of any other NLRI; allow controlled deaggregation, but only of specific routes, and allow export of non-aggregated NLRI; or allow export of only non-aggregated NLRI. The exchange of routing information via EGP2 between a BGP speaker participating in BGP-4 and a pure EGP2 speaker may occur only at the domain boundaries.

The same pattern applies to BGP-3. If the AS_PATH attribute of a BGP-4 route carries AS_SET path segments, the AS_PATH attribute of the BGP-3 route shall be constructed by treating the AS_SET segments as AS_SEQUENCE segments, with the resulting AS_PATH being a single AS_SEQUENCE. While this loses set and sequence information, it does not affect the protection against routing loops, though it may affect policies that are based on the content or ordering of the AS_PATH attribute. The same three injection options are required, and the exchange of routing information via BGP-3 between a BGP speaker participating in BGP-4 and a pure BGP-3 speaker may occur only at the autonomous system boundaries. Within a single autonomous system, BGP conversations between all the BGP speakers of that AS have to be either BGP-3 or BGP-4, but not a mixture.

Section 9 of the document covers running BGP over switched virtual circuit subnetworks, where it may be desirable to eliminate the traffic of periodic KEEPALIVE messages. BGP has a mechanism for operation over switched virtual circuit services that avoids keeping circuits permanently open and eliminates the periodic sending of KEEPALIVE messages. The feature is selected by specifying zero Hold Time in the OPEN message, and it applies only between BGP speakers that are directly connected over a common virtual circuit. The circuit manager must be able to determine link layer unreachability in a predictable finite period, start a configurable dead timer on detecting unreachability, attempt to re-establish the link layer connection, send an internal DEAD indication to TCP if the dead timer expires, and cancel the dead timer and send an UP indication if the connection is re-established. TCP must be modified to process those internal notifications: on DEAD it flushes the transmit queue and aborts the connection, and on UP it transmits any queued data or allows an outgoing call to proceed. If the BGP process and the circuit manager cannot be guaranteed to operate as a single entity, a periodic two-way poll between them should be implemented, so that each can close its connections when the other has gone away.
sections.plainLanguage: During the changeover from BGP-3 and EGP2, a router could speak both, and the document says how information should pass between them, including how to avoid exploding one aggregated route into thousands of individual ones. It also covers running BGP over switched circuits, where the circuit manager tells TCP when the link dies instead of sending keepalives.

viz.caption: The three kinds of autonomous system

items.title: Stub AS
items.text: An AS with only a single connection to one other AS. It naturally carries only local traffic.

items.title: Multihomed AS
items.text: An AS with connections to more than one other AS that refuses to carry transit traffic.

items.title: Transit AS
items.text: An AS with connections to more than one other AS, designed under certain policy restrictions to carry both transit and local traffic.

items.title: Local and transit traffic
items.text: Traffic that starts or ends inside the AS is local traffic. Everything else passing through is transit traffic, and controlling it is a major goal of BGP usage.

viz.caption: The four options for overlapping routes

cells: The less specific route and the more specific route.
No route is installed for the overlapping addresses.

viz.caption: The policies the document gives as examples

items.title: Refuse transit
items.text: A multihomed AS advertises only routes to destinations internal to itself, so it does not act as a transit AS for others.

items.title: Transit for some
items.text: A multihomed AS advertises its routing information to a restricted set of adjacent AS's, so it is a transit AS for them alone.

items.title: Favour or disfavour networks
items.text: An AS can decide which other AS's it prefers to use for carrying its own transit traffic.

items.title: Fewer hops
items.text: An AS can minimise the number of transit AS's by preferring shorter AS paths.

items.title: Quality of the neighbour
items.text: An AS can weigh diameter, link speed, capacity, tendency to congest and quality of operation when it chooses between candidate paths.

items.title: Internal before external
items.text: An AS can express a preference for internal routes over external routes.

viz.caption: What can go into the degree of preference

items.title: AS count
items.text: Paths with a smaller AS count are generally better.

items.title: Policy
items.text: A speaker may know policy constraints within and outside its own AS, and paths that do not comply are not considered further.

items.title: Presence of an AS
items.text: Information from outside BGP, such as bandwidth, MTU or intra-AS diameter, may make some AS's preferable or avoidable.

items.title: Path origin
items.text: A path learned entirely from BGP is generally better than one where part of the path came from EGP or another means.

items.title: AS path subsets
items.text: An AS path that is a subset of a longer path to the same destination should be preferred, since any problem with it is also a problem with the longer one.

items.title: Link dynamics
items.text: Stable paths should be preferred, but this criterion must be used carefully because dynamic information can cause routing instability.
